title: dynamic batching: sequence-length bucketing and padding-minimization heuristics
author: Ava Martinez
release_notes: Improve dynamic batching by bucketing requests by sequence length and minimizing padding. Reduces token cost and improves throughput for mixed-length workloads. Backwards compatible with continuous batching and KV cache semantics.
description: Motivation: Mixed sequence lengths cause excessive padding in batches which increases token compute and memory pressure and can hurt both throughput and tail latency. This PR implements a sequence-length bucketing and padding-minimization heuristic for the serving runtime that reduces wasted tokens while preserving batch formation speed and latency SLOs. Summary of changes: 1) Introduces a lightweight online bucketing component that tracks recent request sequence-length distribution using an EWMA, computes bucket boundaries based on percentile targets, and exposes a fast map from seq_len->bucket_id. 2) Batch formation now prefers grouping requests into the same bucket if it would decrease total padded tokens, but will fall back to cross-bucket batching when latency thresholds are exceeded. 3) Added a small padding-aware cost model to the scheduler which scores candidate batches by padded_tokens * kernel_cost_factor + latency_penalty to trade off cost vs. tail latency. 4) KV-cache alignment: when requests within a bucket share the same model and token-prefix hash, we allow reusing preallocated KV slices to avoid reallocation churn; we also added a cache-coherence check to avoid cache pollution for extremely diverse prefixes. 5) Kernel selection hinting: the batcher now surfaces target padded sequence lengths to the execution layer so the kernel selector can prefer fast-matmul kernels optimized for the resulting padded shapes. 6) Extensive unit and perf tests plus a small docs note. Design notes and trade-offs: Bucketing boundaries are computed to target a configurable percentile (default 80th) to minimize worst-case padding while not exploding the number of small buckets. The EWMA alpha balances responsiveness vs. stability; default alpha set to 0.1 after offline tuning. The batcher uses a hybrid strategy: fast path groups identical buckets; slow path attempts cross-bucket merges only when the expected latency lift is within SLO. This keeps cold-start and request arrival jitter from stalling batch formation. On memory and KV-cache interactions: reusing KV sub-slices significantly reduces allocator pressure for short-prefix workloads at the cost of a small bookkeeping overhead; we observed meaningful improvements in throughput/p99 under realistic traces. Commits summary: "add seqlen bucketer and EWMA profiler; implement bucket-aware batcher and scheduler scoring; add KV-cache alignment logic and reuse paths; kernel hint plumbing and tests; perf tests and docs". Files changed (high level): runtime/scheduler/dynamic_batcher.py (core bucketing and scoring logic); runtime/batching/batcher.rs (batch assembly, fast/slow path); runtime/kv_cache/kv_cache.rs (sub-slice reuse and coherence checks); runtime/execution/kernel_selector.rs (padded-shape hints); tests/perf/test_bucketing.py; tests/unit/test_seqlen_profiler.py; docs/notes/dynamic-batching.md; ci/perf-workflow.yml; examples/benchmarks/mixed_seqlen_workload.yaml. Compatibility: Backwards compatible with existing continuous batching APIs; defaults preserve previous behavior when the feature flag is off. Feature flag: runtime.feature.dynamic_batching_seqlen_enabled (default: true in canary, off in stable). Benchmarks: On a mixed-length web chat trace (15k requests, mean seq_len 120 with heavy tail to 1024) we measured a 32% reduction in padded tokens per batch, a 14% improvement in tokens/sec throughput at 99th percentile latency held constant, and a 12% reduction in GPU memory transient footprint during peaks. For short uniform workloads the difference is negligible. CI and testing: added unit tests that simulate arrival patterns and assert padding reduction and SLO adherence; added perf reproduction deck used in nightly perf workflow. Rollout plan: enable in canary hosts for 2 weeks, monitor per-route padding ratio, cost per token, and p99 latency, then enable for production with opt-out per-application via routing policy. Known limitations and future work: currently bucket IDs are recomputed on alpha-change or after significant distribution shift; future work includes smoother bucket merges/splits, adaptive percentile tuning, and tighter integration with the autoscaler to prefer instances with compatible bucket coverage.
